node-1.label: Patient experienced sudden paralysis beginning in both lower limbs that spread to the trunk and both upper limbs

node-2.label: 25-year-old male of Hispanic and Caucasian descent with no significant past medical history arrived at the emergency department from another facility due to sudden paralysis beginning in both lower limbs

node-3.label: He received an intraarticular corticosteroid injection in his right knee less than 24 hours before symptoms began and consumed a high carbohydrate meal within five hours before onset

node-4.label: Weakness in the lower limbs spread to the trunk and both upper limbs; at the other facility vital signs were normal, and by the time of evaluation he had no symptoms following intravenous correction of low potassium levels

node-5.label: Physical examination revealed paralysis in his limbs, but his sensation remained intact

attrs.why: New laboratory data confirm a hypokalemic periodic paralysis subtype: serum potassium 1.9 mmol/L, suppressed TSH <0.01, elevated free T4 3.73, and elevated TSH receptor antibody 8.60. The laboratory physician interprets this as thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, a subtype of hypokalemic periodic paralysis. Together with the prior corticosteroid/high-carbohydrate triggers and rapid resolution after intravenous potassium, this increases confidence from 0.9 to 0.98.

attrs.why: Serum potassium 1.9 mmol/L demonstrates hypokalemia, while suppressed TSH <0.01, elevated free T4 3.73, and elevated TSH receptor antibody 8.60 indicate thyrotoxicosis/autoimmune thyroid disease. The laboratory physician confirms these findings as thyrotoxic periodic paralysis, and the prior corticosteroid/high-carbohydrate trigger with rapid intravenous potassium response fits this subtype. Confidence is 0.95 because this specific subtype explains the full clinical picture.
